Could she have some knowledge of Yasu's god and the light? Is that the reason why she was so ready to take in Yasu as her own child?
Click to expand...
Now, the following is, admittedly, nothing more than speculation on my part – so take everything that I’m about to say with a grain of salt – but, from my understanding, there are essentially two main reasons for Tsubasa’s strange behavior that can be logically deduced thus far:

The first one is based on a certain quote that Tsubasa says in “For the Sake of Brevity” when discussing this exact topic with Touka – specifically, what she says in response to Touka’s idea of Tsukasa instead marrying one of the staff (which is not ideal, but still better than her being sold to another family) and just generally wondering why it has to be Sensei of all people:

“You understand, Touka – you just don’t want to. The two of you want the same thing, so what’s a mother to do when that happens – especially a mother who’s already promised to protect him, as well? There is only one way to save all of you. And I imagine we’ll all wind up sleeping with him eventually, so what’s the point in holding back now?”

So Tsubasa is not only similar to Ami in that she is fully aware of the whole “Collector” business that is going on with Akira, having come to terms with her own and her daughters’ assigned roles as just three more warm bodies – or, if it was up to someone like HOPE, three more fertile wombs – in Akira’s divinely mandated harem, but she is *also* apparently sworn to watch over Sensei and protect him like a mother, though sworn to whom we don’t yet know.

(The most likely candidate is probably Sekai, considering that whole rumor of how she is apparently buried beneath the everblooming sakura tree inside the Tsukioka Manor. And if that alone isn’t convincing enough, then I could also bring up “The Pleasures of the Flesh”, where Tsubasa explicitly refers to Akira as “Aki-kun” at one point and then follows it up with “you remind me of an old friend when you get passionate like that” in response to him immediately getting agitated, or “When We Dead Awaken”: an event that features multiple allusions to a mysterious third person who is implied to having been inseparable with both Tsubasa and Yuki in the past but "is no longer with them, and will never be”, in addition to the two women repeatedly referencing a lake where they used to hang out as teenagers – which could easily be the same exact lake where Miu, Sekai’s mother, used to live, and thus Sekai herself as well, at least in her childhood.)

Either way, if Tsubasa knows that every single “relevant” woman in Kumon-mi, including her wizard daughter, is effectively bound to sleep with Akira sooner or later and that it all serves some twisted “higher purpose”, then trying to prevent or delay the two of them getting together is essentially pointless, so she might as well play the matchmaker instead to personally oversee and smoothe out the process – which is the second aforementioned reason for Tsubasa’s strange behavior.

Because, ultimately, the reality of their situation is that

a) Tsukasa literally can’t get any older because of the Resets, so she is bound to stay physically a wizard forever

and

b) the thing that makes adult-wizard relationships iffy in the first place is the power imbalance between the two parties due to their inherent mental disparity, but you can’t really apply the same logic to an infinitely-looping world where time is a social construct and a person can be “ten years old” for a millennia straight (like Makoto succinctly put in her monologue in “T Is For Time (Trees & Threes)”)

all of which, pointless morals aside, makes Tsukasa just as bangable as all of the other girls – something that Tsubasa understands and decides to act upon, in no small part for her daughter’s own benefit. At least this way the girl can experience her first time in a somewhat safe environment from a person who clearly knows what he’s doing, and it also has an added benefit of bringing Akira – Tsubasa’s unofficial “ward” – both further under her wing and much closer to the rest of the family, allowing the woman to watch over/control all of her “children” with much greater ease.

How does Yasu fit into all of this (aside from the potential Nozomu/HOPE connection) I’m really not sure. She could not even be involved at all – though that is, admittedly, doubtful.

The issue here is that we only really know the vague general tenets of Yasu’s religion, but not how it actually functions as a proper spiritual movement: we have no idea how many other believers are there, how widespread/publicly accepted it is, if there are any other churches dedicated to Nozomu aside from the abandoned Cathedral (if not in Kumon-mi, then in other Terminals/Wishing Well worlds), is there some financial aspect to the worship (something that is usually the case with similar religious movements IRL, and which could potentially tie this whole thing back to Tsubasa and the Tsukiokas), etcetera – so it’s hard to judge how directly relevant this whole stuff is to the main plot of the game. There is a high chance that Saki (Akira’s mother) was a believer, for example – but, once again, unless Selebus actually confirms this in some future scene, we have only Yasu’s ambiguous words to go off, and she is far from being a 100% reliable source of info. Regardless, the girl’s involvement is a something that cannot be fully answered for now, so I don’t have much to add here, sadly.

spoilers.title: Tsubasa
spoilers.html:
The first one is based on a certain quote that Tsubasa says in “For the Sake of Brevity” when discussing this exact topic with Touka – specifically, what she says in response to Touka’s idea of Tsukasa instead marrying one of the staff (which is not ideal, but still better than her being sold to another family) and just generally wondering why it has to be Sensei of all people:

“You understand, Touka – you just don’t want to. The two of you want the same thing, so what’s a mother to do when that happens – especially a mother who’s already promised to protect him, as well? There is only one way to save all of you. And I imagine we’ll all wind up sleeping with him eventually, so what’s the point in holding back now?”

So Tsubasa is not only similar to Ami in that she is fully aware of the whole “Collector” business that is going on with Akira, having come to terms with her own and her daughters’ assigned roles as just three more warm bodies – or, if it was up to someone like HOPE, three more fertile wombs – in Akira’s divinely mandated harem, but she is *also* apparently sworn to watch over Sensei and protect him like a mother, though sworn to whom we don’t yet know.

(The most likely candidate is probably Sekai, considering that whole rumor of how she is apparently buried beneath the everblooming sakura tree inside the Tsukioka Manor. And if that alone isn’t convincing enough, then I could also bring up “The Pleasures of the Flesh”, where Tsubasa explicitly refers to Akira as “Aki-kun” at one point and then follows it up with “you remind me of an old friend when you get passionate like that” in response to him immediately getting agitated, or “When We Dead Awaken”: an event that features multiple allusions to a mysterious third person who is implied to having been inseparable with both Tsubasa and Yuki in the past but "is no longer with them, and will never be”, in addition to the two women repeatedly referencing a lake where they used to hang out as teenagers – which could easily be the same exact lake where Miu, Sekai’s mother, used to live, and thus Sekai herself as well, at least in her childhood.)

Either way, if Tsubasa knows that every single “relevant” woman in Kumon-mi, including her wizard daughter, is effectively bound to sleep with Akira sooner or later and that it all serves some twisted “higher purpose”, then trying to prevent or delay the two of them getting together is essentially pointless, so she might as well play the matchmaker instead to personally oversee and smoothe out the process – which is the second aforementioned reason for Tsubasa’s strange behavior.

Because, ultimately, the reality of their situation is that

a) Tsukasa literally can’t get any older because of the Resets, so she is bound to stay physically a wizard forever

and

b) the thing that makes adult-wizard relationships iffy in the first place is the power imbalance between the two parties due to their inherent mental disparity, but you can’t really apply the same logic to an infinitely-looping world where time is a social construct and a person can be “ten years old” for a millennia straight (like Makoto succinctly put in her monologue in “T Is For Time (Trees & Threes)”)

all of which, pointless morals aside, makes Tsukasa just as bangable as all of the other girls – something that Tsubasa understands and decides to act upon, in no small part for her daughter’s own benefit. At least this way the girl can experience her first time in a somewhat safe environment from a person who clearly knows what he’s doing, and it also has an added benefit of bringing Akira – Tsubasa’s unofficial “ward” – both further under her wing and much closer to the rest of the family, allowing the woman to watch over/control all of her “children” with much greater ease.

I don't know what your standard for a "great writer" is.
When you read something, what matters are the feelings. This isn't a documentary or a competition with other books.

I binge read this 2 times a year, and in between, I miss the girls as if they are real, close people in my life.
Considering I'm a very stoic stone cold person, the fact that Selebus makes me feel these feelings makes him a great writer to me.

Even looking at it objectively
+Great humor
+35 characters, each with their own interesting personality and story.
+Beautiful citations at the right place and time.
+Metaphors and similes flow perfectly.
+A mystery that still keeps you thinking after years.

Sure, there are a few things I don't like. For example, I hate how he turned adorable Sana into a brainless, boring nympho.
But on the other hand, even though it's sad, I love what Chika turned into. It's exactly what you'd expect her to become in her situation.
The psychological design of the characters is just perfect.
Take Nodoka, for example.
On one hand, she makes you hate her. On the other hand, you feel how sad and vulnerable she is and you just wanna hug her.

I don't like most of the people on here, but at least we can agree on one thing,
Selebus is a great writer, otherwise we wouldn't still be reading after 3 million words

Everybody makes mistakes.
But When you compare the good and bad events, the good ones outweigh the bad ones by a lot.
You might not like the man, but you shouldn't judge his work based on that.

So I suppose that this is as good of an opportunity as any to finally clarify my stance on this matter once and for all, so that history doesn’t repeat itself the fourth time a few weeks/months down the line (once I inevitably cite this event again in one of my future posts).

Firstly, in case this wasn’t extremely clear already: yes, I am firmly of the opinion that what Makoto said to Akira in “T Is For Time (Trees & Threes)” was not only 100% genuine on her part – because she also expresses a very similar “apologist” perspective in a later conversation with Maki in “A Game of Our Own”, which, when combined with her new selfish and detached attitude towards everything (that was brough about by the revelation that they’re all living in an ever-repeating world where consequences are a suggestion and common sense is a joke), definitively paints Makoto in my eyes as someone who is fundamentally amoral: a person who is perfectly willing to disregard any law and commit any sin as long as there is a logically sound justification for doing it – but that it was also one of the most based things she has ever said. And as much as I doubt that it’s even remotely possible for me to convince you of that – since the two of us are fatefully bound to forever disagree about everything – by God (god GOD GoD) am I certainly going to try.

Makoto’s first argument is the same as what I said in my original post: that the main crux of the issue with these relationships is the mental maturity of the underage party – something that humanity, sadly, has not yet found a way to properly measure with any actual degree of accuracy, which is why we unfortunately have to rely on something so crude and arbitrary as deciding on a certain number when a person is supposedly “of age” and then washing our hands away by saying “eh, good enough”. The idea that a person’s “maturity” is inherently tied to their physical age is, frankly, laughable to me: there are countless twenty-, thirty- and forty-year-olds out there who mentally haven’t aged a day past being a teenager, just like there is also an equal number of minors who could have easily cleared the required “mental bar” for a legal right to have sex, if only they were given a chance to – but, once again, since this is a thing that cannot be certifiably measured with any test or by any machine, we choose to err on the side of caution by still basing this entire divide just on physical age (with some additional exceptions for mental disabilities and whatnot), regardless of how imperfect and inaccurate the entire system inherently is.

So here is the million-dollar question then: is there a difference in mental maturity between a teenager who has lived for fifteen years and a teenager who has lived for fifteen hundred years (as obviously impossible and unrealistic as it is)? Makoto argues that, yes, absolutely, because throughout all of those hundreds of years they’re still learning, collecting life experiences and changing as a person, even if their body doesn’t physically grow to reflect that.

If the girls were completely “factory reset” with each loop (like what used to happen with Akira, presumably, and also what Maya went through at the end of Chapter 3) it would have been one thing – because, yes, in that case they would have been permanently stuck whatever age they are both physically and mentally, with no way to evolve past that. This is not what happens, however: in actuality, it’s more accurate to say that everyone in Kumon-me simply has a strong mental block that prevents them from being able to properly judge the passage of time, yet (extremely importantly!) does not prevent them from actually retaining their past memories.

Outside of the few select cases where these memories are actively and intentionally being tempered with (like a “global reset” whenever a “new” Sensei comes around, or stuff like “Bluejay”/Chinami’s illness being retconned out of existence), the characters are perfectly able to remember what happened, just not when it happened, which means that the inherent personal growth that comes from just living your life: learning new skills, forming new relationships, breaking off old ones, and just generally overcoming various challenges that the world throws at you – is very much on the table for all of them. The biological side of it – as in, the physical observable differences in how much the brain is developed between various ages, etcetera – is a handicap, absolutely, but not an insurmountable one: at a certain point a thousand-and-fifteen-years-old teenager and a thousand-and-thirty-year-old adult are not going to be that much mentally different from each other, and when that happens the matter of “not legally being able to give consent” is no longer going to be an issue in any way that truly matters. And that is without even mentioning how the very notion of “consent” is something that was entirely invented by humanity, whereas Kumon-mi is a world made and shaped by the Gods: it’s their divine playground, and they make all the rules. Trying to apply “real world morality” to it all (both by the characters within the story, as well as by us, the readers, outside of it) is a fool’s errand that is bound to end in futility.

Then we have Makoto’s second argument: that throwing Akira into his own personal version of Heaven/Hell that encourages his absolute worst tendencies and then expecting him to just… kind of indefinitely abstain from ever acting on those tendencies is both absurdly unrealistic (since no one has that much self-control) and is also essentially akin to endless torture – which is, hopefully, self-evident enough so that I don’t have to go into any greater detail about why she is very much correct in saying this, leaving only the girl’s third and final point: that both morals and laws only really work in a “carrot-and-a-stick” sort of way (when you’re gaining something for following them: safety, protection, peace of mind, satisfaction of being a “good person”, a promise of afterlife in Heaven, whatever – and losing something for not following them: your freedom, your future, potentially even your life, the sanctity of your soul, etcetera), and when these integral fundamentals are removed – when there is no real reason to be lawful/moral, and no real punishment for being unlawful/immoral – then the entire system just instantly crashes and burns, because it can no longer support its own existence.

The question Makoto was asking Akira back in “T Is For Time (Trees & Threes)” – and the question I’m asking now – is what is the point of Sensei so adamantly continuing to judge himself by the standards of the “old world”, when his current reality is about as far removed from those standards as humanly possible? Kumon-mi is absolutely not a place that cares about laws, morality or common sense: it’s a depraved Wonderland that twists itself to negate any potential consequences of your actions and absolve you from any sin; a city where Gods are real, where wishes and spirits walk among humans, and where time might as well not exist. Yet rather than fully internalize and adapt to these new rules of his eternal day-to-day life – “becoming the best you”, like the members of the Trinity would have called it – Akira is still internally clinging to the same old (now utterly pointless) social labels that have long since lost all of their power: the label of a “criminal”, even though no one will ever convict him of anything; the label of a “predator”, even though the very foundation of how “age” works in Kumon-ni has been completely turned upside-down; the label of a “bad person”, even though there are at least two divine beings who would readily proclaim him to be highly virtuous.

So why continue with this insane self-inflicted mental torture? The endless guilt, the constant regret, the inescapable spiral of self-loathing from trying to uphold yourself to a standard you are inherently incapable of meeting – none of this solves anything or helps Akira move forward in any significant way, only dragging down his already unstable mental state even further into total negativity. So what is the point of doing it? For some abstract notion of “penance”? Fuck that. Why not just discard all of that useless baggage and look at the things from another perspective, accepting that maybe, just maybe, you’re not actually as bad as you make yourself out to be? Or even if you are – who cares? Fucking own it. Be the Big Bad. This is Kumon-mi – no one is going to punish you anyway. The Gods don’t care and neither should you, so pick your poison: embrace the idea of being a victim forced into circumstances beyond your control (which is kind of true, anyway) or just reject morality outright and go balls to the wall on enjoying the insanity – anything is better than infinitely drowning in self-pity and rotting yourself from within, after all.

And secondly, as for your statement that

“The purpose of Makoto's argument in the story is that it's something that Sensei wants/needs to hear, but ultimately isn't true. From things Sel has said on the discord (at least what's been shared here), I would be shocked if he agrees with her.”

the former is just what you think that scene’s purpose is (none of it has been in any way confirmed by the narrative itself as far as I’m aware, so, even if you ultimately end up being correct – which could very well happen, I’m not denying it – currently all we have is just your interpretation of “what it was supposed to mean” versus mine), while the latter is just completely irrelevant as an argument. Selebus is not Makoto: his personal opinions (whatever they may be) do not reflect personal opinions of his characters, and vice-versa. Thus, him agreeing or disagreeing with Makoto on an individual level is a total non-factor in regards to how “correct” she is from an in-universe perspective, because good writers – which I would certainly count Sel as – are not limited by just writing the things that inherently validate their own worldview. Hell, his approach in regards to LiL’s main subject matter speaks for itself in this particular case, since the guy’s adamant hatred of any and all of this stuff IRL – once again, judging by Selebus’ passionate Lilcord posts – doesn’t really seem to influence the text itself in any way: all of the relevant scenes are written with a fuckton of subtlety, nuance and realism, rather than one-sided vitriolic condemnation that is cartoonishly unsubtle in its portrayal (like it usually is in other similar stories).

Either way, I suppose we’ll see.

much self-control) and is also essentially akin to endless torture – which is, hopefully, self-evident enough so that I don’t have to go into any greater detail about why she is very much correct in saying this, leaving only the girl’s third and final point: that both morals and laws only really work in a “carrot-and-a-stick” sort of way (when you’re gaining something for following them: safety, protection, peace of mind, satisfaction of being a “good person”, a promise of afterlife in Heaven, whatever – and losing something for not following them: your freedom, your future, potentially even your life, the sanctity of your soul, etcetera), and when these integral fundamentals are removed – when there is no real reason to be lawful/moral, and no real punishment for being unlawful/immoral – then the entire system just instantly crashes and burns, because it can no longer support its own existence.
The question Makoto was asking Akira back in “T Is For Time (Trees & Threes)” – and the question I’m asking now – is what is the point of Sensei so adamantly continuing to judge himself by the standards of the “old world”, when his current reality is about as far removed from those standards as humanly possible? Kumon-mi is absolutely
not
a place that cares about laws, morality or common sense: it’s a depraved Wonderland that twists itself to negate any potential consequences of your actions and absolve you from any sin; a city where Gods are real, where wishes and spirits walk among humans, and where time might as well not exist. Yet rather than fully internalize and adapt to these new rules of his eternal day-to-day life – “becoming the best you”, like the members of the Trinity would have called it – Akira is still internally clinging to the same old (now utterly pointless) social labels that have long since lost all of their power: the label of a “criminal”, even though no one will ever convict him of anything; the label of a “predator”, even though the very foundation of how “age” works in Kumon-ni has been completely turned upside-down; the label of a “bad person”, even though there are at least two divine beings who would readily proclaim him to be highly virtuous.
So why continue with this insane self-inflicted mental torture? The endless guilt, the constant regret, the inescapable spiral of self-loathing from trying to uphold yourself to a standard you are inherently incapable of meeting – none of this solves anything or helps Akira move forward in any significant way, only dragging down his already unstable mental state even further into total negativity. So what is the point of doing it? For some abstract notion of “penance”? Fuck that. Why not just discard all of that useless baggage and look at the things from another perspective, accepting that maybe, just maybe, you’re not actually as bad as you make yourself out to be? Or even if you are – who cares? Fucking own it. Be the Big Bad. This is Kumon-mi – no one is going to punish you anyway. The Gods don’t care and neither should you, so pick your poison: embrace the idea of being a victim forced into circumstances beyond your control (which
is
kind of true, anyway) or just reject morality outright and go balls to the wall on enjoying the insanity – anything is better than infinitely drowning in self-pity and rotting yourself from within, after all.

spoilers.title: Other stuff
spoilers.html: the former is just what you think that scene’s purpose is (none of it has been in any way confirmed by the narrative itself as far as I’m aware, so, even if you ultimately end up being correct – which could very well happen, I’m not denying it – currently all we have is just your interpretation of “what it was supposed to mean” versus mine), while the latter is just completely irrelevant as an argument. Selebus is not Makoto: his personal opinions (whatever they may be) do not reflect personal opinions of his characters, and vice-versa. Thus, him agreeing or disagreeing with Makoto on an individual level is a total non-factor in regards to how “correct” she is from an in-universe perspective, because good writers – which I would certainly count Sel as – are not limited by just writing the things that inherently validate their own worldview. Hell, his approach in regards to LiL’s main subject matter speaks for itself in this particular case, since the guy’s adamant hatred of any and all of this stuff IRL – once again, judging by Selebus’ passionate Lilcord posts – doesn’t really seem to influence the text itself in any way: all of the relevant scenes are written with a fuckton of subtlety, nuance and realism, rather than one-sided vitriolic condemnation that is cartoonishly unsubtle in its portrayal (like it usually is in other similar stories).

I just got done watching 1000 Dumplings video, and I'm going to make a quick rant post about it. TLDR; I think the video was very good, and I hope to see more in the future.
This video gave me something I have been waiting for and so more. When it comes to long reads like this, I struggle a lot and it was nice to have someone who pieced together some of the topics that were talked about that I didn't notice even on my 2nd playthrough. I know a lot of people are talking about how he reviewed way too early, like literally at the first happy scene, but I honestly think that worked very well. The thing I enjoyed the most out of this video, which is something that I will never be able to replicate myself when it comes to this game, it seeing someone react to the true horrors this game holds, and experience the same or similar emotions I experienced my first time playing this game. This game hits you in a way that I really don't think will be able to be recreated anywhere else, and if it is I'm even more scared at what that would look like.

Another thing people hate on the video for, which I get, is it does seem like they (I don't know their gender and don't care enough to look it up) really take the moral high ground a lot, and constantly reminds the viewers on how fucked up the game is for having terrible content as something people can, and will willingly pay for. Now I do agree with his points to some extent, I think if he brought it up once then let it be would be enough, but he really did hammer it in and that got really annoying. Personally, I literally never looked at the DLC page cause it just looked like filler/non-canon shit so I never really cared, the game itself, especially in the beginning, does a well enough job at reminding me I'm a piece of shit for engaging with this game.

There are some things they get obviously wrong, and I really hope that either A.) They continue with making reviews of the game and maybe get some collaboration going and some high quality theory videos get upload, similar to the deltarune community. Or B.) This video encourages people who either never played the game or saw it as pdf smut to get it a try and the the spreads that way. Sadly, I honestly think both outcomes are extremely unlikely, this game will probably stay underground, for better or for worst. Even when it's fully out I doubt it will ever be allowed to be published to steam, or anywhere else where it would be easily accessible for people with less then half a braincell to acquire it.

Now that the rant is over I do have a genuine question for y'all. How does everyone think of the story, specifically in the recent chapters. I still think it is an amazing game, and I don't think there will be a story that truly tops this one, at least in this genre, for a very long time. However, it does seem like some things tend to be retconned, there seems to be some inconsistencies, and overall I could see it as being sloppy. I think this is just a problem with monthly releases, and I hope by the final product, everything works out and is a cohesive story. I did see on an AMA he did say something along the lines of "there's no hole a good writer can't dig out of" so I do hope he stays true to that. I personally have never had an issue with him, or the game, but I do see a good amount of hate here and just figured I'd ask how y'all feel.

It's funny that you say this, because I posted this near exact opinion a few months back. There were complaints about post 0.54 being slower than usual, not being quite as entertaining.

I had said something about how, since we're all just taking it bit by bit now, we're seeing this as episodic fiction. Much like fanfiction, TV shows, etc, we're getting each new part in chunks, and expecting it to keep our attention like it has in the past. It's simply not possible to do so; as a creator, you sometimes just need to toss out filler to move things along, give a bit of lore and exposition. Not every chapter of a story can be a nerve wracking, cliff hanging, edge of your seat chapter. As a whole piece, that would be EXHAUSTING to read. A story needs ups and downs, otherwise the ups are meaningless.

Essentially, when the game IS done, if the quality as a whole is even half as good as it's best chapters...it's going to be perhaps one of the greatest pieces of fiction ever created. People picking this story up 5-8 years from now, getting the entire thing ready, won't have to suffer the waits and lows that we all will...and I envy them a bit for that. It's much like the transition from normal TV, to being able to binge a show on streaming platforms. Having the complete media is NICE!

So while LIL is amazing, and so much fun...it's worth it to take a break for a few months, and come back when there is another 20 hours to play through. You'll certainly find more enjoyment using that method. If you can put it down, and stay away for an entire year? You definitely should. I wish I could, but I'm sadly very obsessed.

When I picked up LIL, it already had 200 hours of content...I was very lucky! Getting to enjoy LIL in one giant ass chunk was amazing!..but for now I'm stuck theory crafting with the rest of you.

I feel that the overall storyline has become quite depressing since version 0.36, making me very uncomfortable. For example, Ami's unrestrained misdeeds make it hard for me to understand her current character appeal. Chika's madness and the protagonist's constant despondency also make the story feel like it's been stuck in a long period of depression. Maya, my favorite character, has been absent for a long time. (Although the story tries to show that the new Maya and the old Maya are the same character.)

This game brought me a lot of emotion. When I first started playing, I found the author's writing style very unique, and the descriptions of daily life were very interesting, such as the characters' bickering and everyday anecdotes. After version 0.36, I was worried about the author's writing ability, whether they could control the plot well, or whether they would insert personal biases. I'm glad to see the storyline improving recently.

(I am a Chinese player. The most accurate unofficial translation of Lil is currently version 0.39. I am using OCR and a translator to play the game.)

Of all the weird little things to run into...
I am in the middle of a replay, and I still have and play the "1999 PC Classic, Rollercoaster Tycoon"
During this event Sensai says that he can "turn the game volume up"... this is actually impossible, there is no volume control in the game, at all... this is because at the time all PC's had external speakers with physical volume controls on them. In game, you can mute or unmute the sounds, that is it.
If you want to actually play RollerCoaster Tycoon <proper spelling> then you can get it really cheap on GoG, and they provide an offline installer that still works with Win11.

How does everyone think of the story, specifically in the recent chapters. I still think it is an amazing game, and I don't think there will be a story that truly tops this one, at least in this genre, for a very long time. However, it does seem like some things tend to be retconned, there seems to be some inconsistencies, and overall I could see it as being sloppy. I think this is just a problem with monthly releases, and I hope by the final product, everything works out and is a cohesive story. I did see on an AMA he did say something along the lines of "there's no hole a good writer can't dig out of" so I do hope he stays true to that. I personally have never had an issue with him, or the game, but I do see a good amount of hate here and just figured I'd ask how y'all feel.
Click to expand...
As time goes by, I mind less and less about retcon, understanding that it is nigh impossible to not have any inconsistency in a game this size, and what I'd consider inconsistency could very well be my own personal take on things deliberately kept vague in the first place. However, even when intentionally looking past any potential retcon, the most recent chapter still remains far less memorable than prior ones and that imo has always been the bigger problem.

Chapter1-3 have been quite concise, engaging, and steadily intriguing, to a point that most of us can easily remember sequences, quotes, or even soundtracks of most events because everything feels like we were really going somewhere. Chapter4? A jumbled mess that is supposedly all according to the plan. Much larger in size and much less in progress when major strides are more expected than ever. There are just so many forgettable nothingburgers here and there in Chapter4 that they make even the rare shiny moments a lot more forgettable than they deserve. While writing this post, I just found out myself forgetting about almost the entire existence of the 5th dorm wars.

As always, I blame this significantly worse viewing experience majorly on the ridiculously long timeline and the gigantic roadmap he set for this game that forces himself to stall, and make inconsistent crap to fill the blank before the good stuff is (in his book) ready to kick in. Monthly release only exacerbates this entire situation. While it might be true that Chapter4 is deliberately designed to be both dreading, dragging, and depressing due to story reasons, and maybe replaying the entire Chapter4 in one continuous sitting would give it better justice, well as of now this design simply sucks balls as I honestly don't see which part of it is made to be more appealing than the prior chapters. All in all, a 11/10 game with an amazing start and buildup but is also undergoing its midlife crisis. Get out of the hole and leave dorm wars in the hole Selly!

I think it's been a year since I last played this VN, interesting to see that many of my conjectures were correct
Has the "dark phase" already begun? How "denpa" has it become?

Because, if we put it into perspective, some exponents of this genre are quite grotesque;
Rape, suicide, and murder are so common that they get even more exaggerated just for the shock value

Idk if anyone else already pointed but it's interesting to see the similarities of this VN with Wonderful Everyday, probably the most popular VN of the denpa genre, like the focus on school rooftops (and JUMPing from it), "world ending" events, the many literary references and philosophical talks (heavily focused on cynicism and nihilism)...

The point is, if that VN is any indication of what's to come... yeah... a lot of people won't take it very well

I find it kind of funny that you listed all of those (honestly fairly generic) narrative parallels between these two works without ever bringing up the two most overt SubaHibi connections: the thematic focus on “being happy” (“Live happily!” and “Remember to smile!” are not that far apart in their intended meanings, after all) as well as the importance of sunflowers as an integral story motif (hell, to go even further on the similarities, Akira references a “field of sunflowers” on at least five separate occasions throughout the entire game thus far) – the latter of which is especially funny, because, if I remember correctly, the only time Selebus ever mentioned the word “Himawari” in his Discord server prior to the release of version 0.53 (or maybe even since then, I dunno) was when he was speaking about a SubaHibi song that had “sunflower” in its name.

That being said, though – and with an added caveat that it has been quite a long time since I last read Wonderful Everyday, so there is a decently high chance that my current memories and impressions of it might not really be all that accurate – I don’t really believe that the two stories are actually that much alike:

Wonderful Everyday fundamentally strikes me as a very optimistic story at its core: a story that ultimately condemns all of the “bad” stuff that happens within it and argues that it’s just the unfortunate result of people not knowing how to “live happily” rather than something that is inherent to humanity as a whole – the “cynicism and nihilism” you attribute to it are actually much more strongly present in Tsui no Sora, SubaHibi’s “progenitor” project with a very different narrative focus and thematic message, whereas SubaHibi itself openly wants you to always try to look on the brighter side of things. Lessons in Love, meanwhile, is… much more “neutral” in its messaging, perfectly signified by Edgar Allan Poe’s “there is no beauty without some strangeness in its proportions” quote that the game essentially opens with, which might as well be LiL’s core ideological thesis, alongside all of the ideas of “perception” and how it shapes both us and the world around us. Though I already spoke on this subject at length in many of my mega-essays – the post-Christmas “Nodoka as a group therapist” one especially (where I also directly referenced SubaHibi at one point, funnily enough) – so I won’t waste anyone’s time by pointlessly repeating myself here.

At the end of the day, SCA-DI and Selebus are two very, very different authors, and the ways in which they tackle similar themes, tropes, plot points and characters only partially overlap. And as far as "if that VN is any indication of what's to come... yeah... a lot of people won't take it very well" goes: I don't think we will ever get anything even remotely on the level of batshit depraved insanity that was going on in the second half of "It's my Own Invention" (at least I think that the dog scene and the teacher scene were from that chapter, or perhaps I'm partially mixing it with "Looking-glass Insects"?), but, conversely, I also don't think that SCA-DI could have ever written anything as phenomenal as "Stomachache", so... I guess we'll see.

Lessons in Love, meanwhile, is… much more “neutral” in its messaging, perfectly signified by Edgar Allan Poe’s “there is no beauty without some strangeness in its proportions” quote that the game essentially opens with, which might as well be LiL’s core ideological thesis, alongside all of the ideas of “perception” and how it shapes both us and the world around us. Though I already spoke on this subject at length in many of my mega-essays – the post-Christmas “Nodoka as a group therapist” one especially (where I also directly referenced SubaHibi at one point, funnily enough) – so I won’t waste anyone’s time by pointlessly repeating myself here.
At the end of the day, SCA-DI and Selebus are two very, very different authors, and the ways in which they tackle similar themes, tropes, plot points and characters only partially overlap. And as far as "
if that VN is any indication of what's to come... yeah... a lot of people won't take it very well

ever

that the dog scene and the teacher scene were from that chapter, or perhaps I'm partially mixing it with "Looking-glass Insects"?), but, conversely, I also don't think that SCA-DI could have ever written anything as phenomenal as "Stomachache", so... I guess we'll see.

I wrote a small mod that lets you skip the affection/lust point grind without having to go through the tedium of typing in cheat codes or having your save labelled with the cheater flag.

View attachment 1901303

Features:
  • Sets all girls' affection and lust points to a value X unless they were already higher than X
  • Can set a specific girl's love/lust points
  • Written to be future-proof (i.e. will automatically work for any new girls, you will never need to update the mod)
  • Enables the developer console
Usage Instructions:
  • Download the attached file
    • Note: if you get sent to a new tab with a bunch of text, just right click and hit "Save as" and name it as z_set_love_lust.rpy
  • Move into the folder named "game" (found inside the folder that you launch Lessons in Love from)
  • Load a save and open the developer console with Shift + O
  • Press Enter a few times until you can see the ">" symbol in the top left of the screen
  • To update all girls' love and lust: type setLoveAndLust(X) and press Enter(for an example, see the image below)
    • Note: X must be an integer (aka whole number)
  • To update a specific girl's love or lust, for example Ami: type "ami_love += X" and/or "ami_lust += X" without the quotation marks and then press Enter.
    • Note: the girl's name must be fully lower-case.
    • This will increase their love/lust by X. If you want to make it equal to X then omit the plus sign
  • Press Esc to close the console and now you can play!

Bonus stuff (not essential to read):

I recommend using this with the guide mod for max efficiency because other than grinding points, the main time-sink with this game is trying to trigger events.

If you want a version of the mod that lets you set affection and lust points separately (useful if you don't want to see any lust events), see here: https://f95zone.to/threads/lessons-in-love-v0-30-0-selebus.48158/post-10770605

Advice from alex2011 on how to use the mod so that you don't accidentally miss events (note: I used the mod myself with 50 affection from the start and didn't experience any issues. You can still miss events even if you follow the instructions below and you can still see all events while ignoring those instructions.):


Uninstall: delete the files z_set_love_lust.rpy and z_set_love_lust.rpyc from your game subfolder

Edit: I tried writing a super long post about how I've been rethinking my approach to LiL, but I don't have that capacity anymore apparently. The general idea was that maybe there's a middleground between "either Selebus knows what he's doing or doesn't".
I've been thinking that it's more like a long running manga series that the author sort of knows what the ending is supposed to be, but almost everything in the middle is side-questing made on the fly - sometimes very good, sometimes trash, overall decent. And by that token you don't really have to scrutinize most of the story other than the main (very minimal and rare) plot.

Just one point I think might be worth thinking about, even with that approach, is the lack of any real consequence to the character arcs. LiL is reminiscent of a soap opera, but one where, no matter what, every single character will get their perfect ending... so, I mean... I like Yumi and I want her to be happy. But does it really matter if at the end she'll just get a second perfect life? In other words: "does it matter beyond the fact that I don't want to see her suffering momentarily right now"?

At the grand scheme of things does it even matter that Yuki got hurt? Even if I'm seeing the one instance out of a billion where that either happened or didn't, and she's going to have a perfect life by the end regardless? Cause if it doesn't matter, then isn't it just about being happy when the moments that you want to happen do happen? And being pleasantly surprised sometimes or inclined to ignore something you didn't want to see in specific events?
These are some of the questions I had about LiL while being away. Maybe they resonate with someone. I also have no update on my current health condition unfortunately.

That being said, though – and with an added caveat that it has been quite a long time since I last read Wonderful Everyday, so there is a decently high chance that my current memories and impressions of it might not really be all that accurate – I don’t really believe that the two stories are actually that much alike:

Wonderful Everyday fundamentally strikes me as a very optimistic story at its core: a story that ultimately condemns all of the “bad” stuff that happens within it and argues that it’s just the unfortunate result of people not knowing how to “live happily” rather than something that is inherent to humanity as a whole – the “cynicism and nihilism” you attribute to it are actually much more strongly present in Tsui no Sora, SubaHibi’s “progenitor” project with a very different narrative focus and thematic message, whereas SubaHibi itself openly wants you to always try to look on the brighter side of things. Almost done with version .57 and I’m curious. Does anyone know what the game would be like if you only had sex with the adults. Because right now the story is almost fully based around the adults confronting you about having sex with the class so I wonder just how drastically different it is

Assuming "you" refers to Sensei, and he never went after minors, then the World Itself likely wouldn't exist. Himawari wouldn't exist. Maya probably wouldn't exist. And the original Sensei would probably be married with original Niki. Etc. At least taking the known lore into account.

If Sensei wasn't a pedo, then this game would have to be completely rewritten. (Even if he was only an Ephebophile, it'd probably change everything.)

If Sensei just started to only want grown women, then he'd probably get replaced by the next Sensei eventually, since the whole "complete the collection" thing seems to be one of his only reasons for being around lore wise. There's also apparently "landmarks" he has to experience, so even going after the adults would probably just cause him to glitch out and rape some of the teens, at times. He's already made his choice as is said sometimes.

Moonflare said:
A game sold on steam.

Edit: I tried writing a super long post about how I've been rethinking my approach to LiL, but I don't have that capacity anymore apparently. The general idea was that maybe there's a middleground between "either Selebus knows what he's doing or doesn't".
I've been thinking that it's more like a long running manga series that the author sort of knows what the ending is supposed to be, but almost everything in the middle is side-questing made on the fly - sometimes very good, sometimes trash, overall decent. And by that token you don't really have to scrutinize most of the story other than the main (very minimal and rare) plot.

Just one point I think might be worth thinking about, even with that approach, is the lack of any real consequence to the character arcs. LiL is reminiscent of a soap opera, but one where, no matter what, every single character will get their perfect ending... so, I mean... I like Yumi and I want her to be happy. But does it really matter if at the end she'll just get a second perfect life? In other words: "does it matter beyond the fact that I don't want to see her suffering momentarily right now"?

At the grand scheme of things does it even matter that Yuki got hurt? Even if I'm seeing the one instance out of a billion where that either happened or didn't, and she's going to have a perfect life by the end regardless? Cause if it doesn't matter, then isn't it just about being happy when the moments that you want to happen do happen? And being pleasantly surprised sometimes or inclined to ignore something you didn't want to see in specific events?
These are some of the questions I had about LiL while being away. Maybe they resonate with someone. I also have no update on my current health condition unfortunately.
Click to expand...
Considering the "Happy Ends"/Purity Routes aren't the True End, I don't think there's any guarantee this is going to end happily ever after for anyone. Even Himawari's Wish-World idea seems deeply flawed. After all, her own perfect wish-world isn't enough for her...and Maya's is, well, a mess that is basically her hell. Be careful what you wish for, etc.

I suppose if any version of them in any world getting a decent life is all one could want for them, then it'll probably end alright. (Unless Sel pulls a Crisis on Infinite Earths. Erasing even the happily ever afters at the time for like 40 years Irl. Or a House of M: "No more wish-worlds")

Overall: "Yesterday is history, tomorrow is a mystery, but today is a gift. That is why it is called the present."

What the characters go through now will affect us now, and how their stories might end shouldn't be the focus. I mean, for all we know, Sel might abandon the game or get in a car crash and reincarnate as Kaori. There may not even be an end, in the end.

if the last update you played was 0.11 then there's definitely been some serious changes since.
0.11 was the end of what is now chapter 1 and since then we have seen the introduction of about 20 new main/side cast, 3 full chapters of increasing scale, a rewrite of most of chapter 1 in an attempt to bring it up to the standard Sel wanted, and a hell of a lot more. The writing has definitely had its ups and downs, especially recently,but i would definitely say that the last few updates have me hopeful that things are heading in the right direction, at least for now.
As for your queries about the 'vibes' surrounding the game, there are 3 main english-speaking communities that i know of (i understand there are fairly sizable chinese and russian communities too but i dont speak either language so i have no idea what they think of the game):
this thread still draws in new people from time to time, although i would say it's pretty infrequent, and the general consensus seems to be that bashing Selebus is completely fair game, especially if an update fails to measure up in terms of quality.
The official discord is mostly populated by Sel's patreons and tends to be significantly more sycophantic in their views of the game, plus they have a weird thing against giving out answers to puzzles for some reason.
Recently there's also been a fairly sizable group of new players being introduced to the game through a thread being run on 4chan's /vg/ board because apparently the game got popular enough that people on the thread for western VNs started complaining about the number of people posting LiL, so someone decided to make it its own thread.
I dont really check on it very often but it looks like the majority of them are still pretty early in the story so im not particularly sure what they really think of the game as a whole.
Overall, to adress your main 3 concerns of quality, pacing and atmosphere, I would definitely say that the quality of the writing has increased drastically, and it would probably be worth replaying chapter 1 to experience the rewrite.
As for the pacing, it's had some rough spots recently, but chapters 2 and 3, despite their length, kept me pretty engaged for most of the time, although some character arcs *cough cough* futaba *cough cough* definitely took far longer than they really should have.
Atmosphere I would say remains mostly similar but growing increasingly darker until around the end of chapter 3, when the game takes a hard shift (that is and was rather controversial) into a significantly more absurdist atmosphere, especially around the happy events.
I would definitely say a reread is worth it, probably starting from the beginning.
My last reread was around a year ago now, and I was caught up in around 6 weeks or so reading an hour or two a day, so a read at that pace now would probably take around 2 months or so to be fully caught up.
One piece of advice i would offer is using the mods linked in the original post and URM to significantly reduce the need for grinding in the sandbox sections and searching the wiki for event triggers, or just use the auto-vn mod if that's more your speed.

this thread still draws in new people from time to time, although i would say it's pretty infrequent, and the general consensus seems to be that bashing Selebus is completely fair game, especially if an update fails to measure up in terms of quality.

There was a moment in 0.58 which I'm surprised no one has brought up for discussion, because I think it's a pretty big lore reveal: Maya's wizard memory (assuming it's genuine) confirmed that she met Ami back in the old district (at Akira's house, in fact).


(Technically Maya never said she met Ami, only that she saw what she likes like. But I don't think any alternate explanation makes sense in the context of the conversation. I can go into more detail on that if anyone disagrees.)
At least in theory, this should have come as a surprise, as it contradicts the official story. Ami said she met Maya in middle school (after leaving the old district) and (as far as Ami knows) it was Ami who introduced Akira to Maya, rather than the other way around.


Whether or not Ami actually believes this, it seems like Maya and Akira expected her to - Maya pretended not to know Ami while (re-)befriending her so that she'd have an excuse to spend time at Akira's house while still hiding their relationship from Ami.
But from Maya's memory, in actuality Akira introduced Maya to Ami sometime before that, which Ami (supposedly) doesn't remember.
Ami herself may have unknowingly talked about this first meeting, when she told Sensei about a play date she had at his house with a girl she can't quite remember. I think Maya's memory all but confirms that she was that mystery girl.
(for context: they're talking about Noriko)
To summarize: Maya remembers meeting Ami at Sensei's house in the old district. Ami doesn't remember that, but she does remember meeting a mystery girl at Sensei's house in the old district. It would be an outrageous coincidence (and a bizarre narrative choice) if these weren't the same meeting.

This now brings me to the real reason I'm writing this post, the reason that it's important that Maya was the mystery girl: Ami's play date happened before the accident. If the play date was with Maya, it means Maya existed before the accident, which means Akira made his wish before the accident.
Ami brings up the play date in the context of Sensei's "old house", the one that he lived in without Ami. She also says it happened when she "visited" the house. So it happened before the two of them lived together.

Ami and Sensei have lived together since the accident; she was seven years old and he was her new legal guardian. Ami has described how Sensei went catatonic after the accident, and the two of them holed up in their house while she took care of him.







So there's no point in time after the accident when Ami could have visited a house that Akira lived in alone.


While we're here, there's one more (much weaker) clue in 0.58 that Maya was around before the accident. She told Niki that she watched Akira break (due to lost love) with her own eyes. She's talking about how he lost Sekai, and she implies she saw how it changed him instead of just meeting him in the aftermath.
This could just be weirdly phrased, so I don't think it's very strong evidence on its own, but it points in the same direction.
Before I go further I should mention that there's a few fishy things going on in Maya's memory, so it's possible it isn't real, though I believe that it is.
1. It contradicts Maya's "memory" from when she jumped through time at Halloween. In that scene, wizard Maya brings up Ami to Sensei, and he reacts like she shouldn't know about her.
This is a fake Sensei rather than a true memory, so maybe it's meaningless, but I don't know why Sel would include it in that case.

2. Maya herself may be unsure if the memory is genuine. Later in the update she tells Sensei she wants to talk to him about a "weird dream" she had, rather than about something she remembered.

3. During the memory, we can see a couple things that couldn't have actually been there in a real event.
- Maya is drawing Ami, and Akira says it's a good likeness, but we get a glance at her paper and it appears that she's actually drawing Wilford Blackhole Hands (Maybe this should tell us something interesting about Ami, but I have no idea what).

- Wizard Noriko is visible in the background, but the conversation makes it obvious that Akira and Maya are alone.

4. Sensei's face in the memory is blurred like she can't really remember him, even though she has said everything about her relationship with Akira is very clear in her mind. This could mean nothing, but maybe it's an indication that this is a different Akira than the one she remembers.

5. The memory taks place when Maya was no older than 10, but she shows a surprising amount of emotional maturity and uses complex metaphors. I don't think any 10-year-old, even a very bright one, would talk like that. But I'm no expert, and maybe Sel thinks otherwise.


Despite those points, I doubt the memory is completely fake. I can't see what narrative purpose that would serve, nor do I know why someone would show it to her if it isn't real. If anything, it's possible it's New Maya's own memories that are the fakes, because someone (probably the gods) don't want her to remember how things really started.

It might not be coincidence that Maya recovers this memory during the "Drawing With Nao-chan" event. The last time the two of them interacted ("Nao More Than Ever"), Nao-chan was trying to help Maya remember who she is. She might have helped her with another memory this time around, though I didn't notice anything directly hinting at that in the event.


That being said, let's talk about Maya before the accident. This isn't the first time I've written about it. This post has other evidence that she was around, along with speculation about Sekai's role in her relationship with Akira. I also shared a very speculative theory about Maya, Sekai, and the scary room here.

Since those posts, Himawari has revealed some very important context about wishes and Maya's past, so it's worth revisiting the subject.
If we want to consider Maya before the accident, I think there are three big questions to focus on.
  1. What was her relationship with Akira?
  2. What was Akira's wish, and when did he make it?
  3. How was Sekai involved (if at all) in her life?
I'll share my latest thoughts on all three of these, but these are very much subject to change.

1. Maya and Akira before the accident
We already have good reason to believe that nothing sexual happened before the accident: from the stories in sleepsong.mp3 (Maya's voice talking about "falling into you") and amibreak4.png (the green scarf story), the timeline seems to be:
  1. Maya starts to fall in love with Akira, but thinks her love is hopeless.
  2. The accident happens and Akira loses both of his lovers.
  3. Sometime later she admits her feelings and he thinks about it for three weeks before reciprocating.
But that doesn't tell us a lot about Akira's intentions, especially when these stories are coming from someone who was a young child at the time. He easily could have been grooming her for a relationship for a long time before it actually happened.

I think the new evidence suggests this wasn't the case, that Akira really did intend for his relationship with Maya to be innocent. In the memory, Akira says he can't let Maya come to his house because he has to hide her - he knows he's doing something very wrong and very illegal, and he has to keep it a secret. But this wasn't always the case, as he previously let her meet Ami and spend time at his house. To me, the obvious reason this changed is because of the start of their sexual relationship. Before that point, Akira didn't feel the need to hide her. Crucially, though, this also speaks to his intent; if he was always planning to turn the relationship sexual, he would have known from the beginning that he needed to keep it a secret.

So at the moment I lean toward the interpretation that Akira had good intentions for Maya, that he genuinely wanted to help a homeless girl, and things only went wrong after the accident broke him.


2. Akira's wish
From the way Himawari explained wishes that create people, my interpretation is that these wishes don't change the timeline (think also of how Kaori's wish added Nao to Sensei's timeline). So if Maya existed before the accident, Akira almost certainly wished for her before the accident (Technically there's an alternative - Akira wishes for Maya after the accident, then sometime later the world resets to before the accident, bringing Maya along because she's now a permanent part of the world. But I have no idea why Sel would do that.). That throws a wrench in the most popular theory of Akira's wish, that he was desperately lonely and/or horny after the accident and wished for a new (loli) girlfriend.

The stuff I wrote above about Akira's intentions also suggest that the wish wasn't sexual, though it's not conclusive. (We've seen with his treatment of Tsukasa that he's capable of consciously wanting to do the right thing at the same time that he grooms a wizard he's lusting for.) But I also tend to think a sexual wish is a lot less likely before the accident, when Akira is getting all he wants from two different "girlfriends".

I think it's more likely he was looking for someone to save. Hence Maya's backstory as a victim of abuse alone in the world. He sees himself in her and wants to save her the same way he credits Sekai with saving him - but only partially. Because while he loves Sekai for saving him from his abusive family and giving him something to live for, he also blames her for stealing his innocence/childhood. With Maya, he wanted to show that he could provide the good without the bad - but he failed.

I wonder if there's another element as well: maybe he wanted a "daughter" he could raise in place of his real one. It's very likely that Akira knew or at least heavily suspected that Ami was his biological daughter, but he didn't get to act like her father before the accident. (Ami has said she saw him occasionally back then, but they had no real relationship.) Maybe that was his choice, but I heavily doubt it - Akira's desire to be a father is a major aspect of his character (even if he also rejects it at times). He became a tutor and later a teacher because he wants to help kids.

So then why did he stay away from Ami? It seems to me that must have been Sekai's choice, that for whatever reason she wanted Ami to grow up with Nozomu very firmly in the father role. Akira may have desired that relationship and looked to Maya as a surrogate daughter. This could also play into why Narrator Ami thinks Maya stole her "story".


3. Sekai and Maya
We didn't get any more hints about how they interacted, but if Ami's play date really was with Maya, it reinforces my conviction that Sekai knew about her. Surely she must have known why Ami was going to Akira's house, especially since he wasn't trying to hide Maya at that point. And even if she somehow didn't know, Ami would have told her about her play date after it happened, raising the obvious question of why another little girl is at Akira's house.

The exact nature of their relationship remains to be seen, but I think it's going to be important.
So what do you think - am I over-reading something that could be a continuity error? Do you think the memory is fake, or do you have an alternate explanation for Maya's knowledge of Ami? How about any thoughts on Maya before the accident?

If we want to consider Maya before the accident, I think there are three big questions to focus on.
  1. What was her relationship with Akira?
  2. What was Akira's wish, and when did he make it?
  3. How was Sekai involved (if at all) in her life?
I'll share my latest thoughts on all three of these, but these are very much subject to change.

1. Maya and Akira before the accident
We already have good reason to believe that nothing sexual happened before the accident: from the stories in sleepsong.mp3 (Maya's voice talking about "falling into you") and amibreak4.png (the green scarf story), the timeline seems to be:
  1. Maya starts to fall in love with Akira, but thinks her love is hopeless.
  2. The accident happens and Akira loses both of his lovers.
  3. Sometime later she admits her feelings and he thinks about it for three weeks before reciprocating.
But that doesn't tell us a lot about Akira's intentions, especially when these stories are coming from someone who was a young child at the time. He easily could have been grooming her for a relationship for a long time before it actually happened.

I think the new evidence suggests this wasn't the case, that Akira really did intend for his relationship with Maya to be innocent. In the memory, Akira says he can't let Maya come to his house because he has to hide her - he knows he's doing something very wrong and very illegal, and he has to keep it a secret. But this wasn't always the case, as he previously let her meet Ami and spend time at his house. To me, the obvious reason this changed is because of the start of their sexual relationship. Before that point, Akira didn't feel the need to hide her. Crucially, though, this also speaks to his intent; if he was always planning to turn the relationship sexual, he would have known from the beginning that he needed to keep it a secret.

So at the moment I lean toward the interpretation that Akira had good intentions for Maya, that he genuinely wanted to help a homeless girl, and things only went wrong after the accident broke him.


2. Akira's wish
From the way Himawari explained wishes that create people, my interpretation is that these wishes don't change the timeline (think also of how Kaori's wish added Nao to Sensei's timeline). So if Maya existed before the accident, Akira almost certainly wished for her before the accident (Technically there's an alternative - Akira wishes for Maya after the accident, then sometime later the world resets to before the accident, bringing Maya along because she's now a permanent part of the world. But I have no idea why Sel would do that.). That throws a wrench in the most popular theory of Akira's wish, that he was desperately lonely and/or horny after the accident and wished for a new (loli) girlfriend.

The stuff I wrote above about Akira's intentions also suggest that the wish wasn't sexual, though it's not conclusive. (We've seen with his treatment of Tsukasa that he's capable of consciously wanting to do the right thing at the same time that he grooms a wizard he's lusting for.) But I also tend to think a sexual wish is a lot less likely before the accident, when Akira is getting all he wants from two different "girlfriends".

I think it's more likely he was looking for someone to save. Hence Maya's backstory as a victim of abuse alone in the world. He sees himself in her and wants to save her the same way he credits Sekai with saving him - but only partially. Because while he loves Sekai for saving him from his abusive family and giving him something to live for, he also blames her for stealing his innocence/childhood. With Maya, he wanted to show that he could provide the good without the bad - but he failed.

I wonder if there's another element as well: maybe he wanted a "daughter" he could raise in place of his real one. It's very likely that Akira knew or at least heavily suspected that Ami was his biological daughter, but he didn't get to act like her father before the accident. (Ami has said she saw him occasionally back then, but they had no real relationship.) Maybe that was his choice, but I heavily doubt it - Akira's desire to be a father is a major aspect of his character (even if he also rejects it at times). He became a tutor and later a teacher because he wants to help kids.

So then why did he stay away from Ami? It seems to me that must have been Sekai's choice, that for whatever reason she wanted Ami to grow up with Nozomu very firmly in the father role. Akira may have desired that relationship and looked to Maya as a surrogate daughter. This could also play into why Narrator Ami thinks Maya stole her "story".


3. Sekai and Maya
We didn't get any more hints about how they interacted, but if Ami's play date really was with Maya, it reinforces my conviction that Sekai knew about her. Surely she must have known why Ami was going to Akira's house, especially since he wasn't trying to hide Maya at that point. And even if she somehow didn't know, Ami would have told her about her play date after it happened, raising the obvious question of why another little girl is at Akira's house.

The exact nature of their relationship remains to be seen, but I think it's going to be important.

aramaug said:
There was a moment in 0.58 which I'm surprised no one has brought up for discussion, because I think it's a pretty big lore reveal: Maya's wizard memory (assuming it's genuine) confirmed that she met Ami back in the old district (at Akira's house, in fact).
View attachment 6130842 View attachment 6130843 View attachment 6130844 View attachment 6130847

(Technically Maya never said she met Ami, only that she saw what she likes like. But I don't think any alternate explanation makes sense in the context of the conversation. I can go into more detail on that if anyone disagrees.)
At least in theory, this should have come as a surprise, as it contradicts the official story. Ami said she met Maya in middle school (after leaving the old district) and (as far as Ami knows) it was Ami who introduced Akira to Maya, rather than the other way around.
View attachment 6130817 View attachment 6130820

Whether or not Ami actually believes this, it seems like Maya and Akira expected her to - Maya pretended not to know Ami while (re-)befriending her so that she'd have an excuse to spend time at Akira's house while still hiding their relationship from Ami.
But from Maya's memory, in actuality Akira introduced Maya to Ami sometime before that, which Ami (supposedly) doesn't remember.
Ami herself may have unknowingly talked about this first meeting, when she told Sensei about a play date she had at his house with a girl she can't quite remember. I think Maya's memory all but confirms that she was that mystery girl.
(for context: they're talking about Noriko)
View attachment 6130824 View attachment 6130827
To summarize: Maya remembers meeting Ami at Sensei's house in the old district. Ami doesn't remember that, but she does remember meeting a mystery girl at Sensei's house in the old district. It would be an outrageous coincidence (and a bizarre narrative choice) if these weren't the same meeting.

This now brings me to the real reason I'm writing this post, the reason that it's important that Maya was the mystery girl: Ami's play date happened before the accident. If the play date was with Maya, it means Maya existed before the accident, which means Akira made his wish before the accident.
Ami brings up the play date in the context of Sensei's "old house", the one that he lived in without Ami. She also says it happened when she "visited" the house. So it happened before the two of them lived together.

Ami and Sensei have lived together since the accident; she was seven years old and he was her new legal guardian. Ami has described how Sensei went catatonic after the accident, and the two of them holed up in their house while she took care of him.
View attachment 6130835 View attachment 6130837


View attachment 6130807 View attachment 6130808 View attachment 6130811
View attachment 6130812 View attachment 6130814 View attachment 6130816


View attachment 6130838
So there's no point in time after the accident when Ami could have visited a house that Akira lived in alone.


While we're here, there's one more (much weaker) clue in 0.58 that Maya was around before the accident. She told Niki that she watched Akira break (due to lost love) with her own eyes. She's talking about how he lost Sekai, and she implies she saw how it changed him instead of just meeting him in the aftermath.
View attachment 6130849 View attachment 6130852
This could just be weirdly phrased, so I don't think it's very strong evidence on its own, but it points in the same direction.
Before I go further I should mention that there's a few fishy things going on in Maya's memory, so it's possible it isn't real, though I believe that it is.
1. It contradicts Maya's "memory" from when she jumped through time at Halloween. In that scene, wizard Maya brings up Ami to Sensei, and he reacts like she shouldn't know about her.
View attachment 6130853 View attachment 6130856
This is a fake Sensei rather than a true memory, so maybe it's meaningless, but I don't know why Sel would include it in that case.

2. Maya herself may be unsure if the memory is genuine. Later in the update she tells Sensei she wants to talk to him about a "weird dream" she had, rather than about something she remembered.

3. During the memory, we can see a couple things that couldn't have actually been there in a real event.
- Maya is drawing Ami, and Akira says it's a good likeness, but we get a glance at her paper and it appears that she's actually drawing Wilford Blackhole Hands (Maybe this should tell us something interesting about Ami, but I have no idea what).
View attachment 6130857
View attachment 6130882 View attachment 6130895
- Wizard Noriko is visible in the background, but the conversation makes it obvious that Akira and Maya are alone.
View attachment 6130901

4. Sensei's face in the memory is blurred like she can't really remember him, even though she has said everything about her relationship with Akira is very clear in her mind. This could mean nothing, but maybe it's an indication that this is a different Akira than the one she remembers.

5. The memory taks place when Maya was no older than 10, but she shows a surprising amount of emotional maturity and uses complex metaphors. I don't think any 10-year-old, even a very bright one, would talk like that. But I'm no expert, and maybe Sel thinks otherwise.


Despite those points, I doubt the memory is completely fake. I can't see what narrative purpose that would serve, nor do I know why someone would show it to her if it isn't real. If anything, it's possible it's New Maya's own memories that are the fakes, because someone (probably the gods) don't want her to remember how things really started.

It might not be coincidence that Maya recovers this memory during the "Drawing With Nao-chan" event. The last time the two of them interacted ("Nao More Than Ever"), Nao-chan was trying to help Maya remember who she is. She might have helped her with another memory this time around, though I didn't notice anything directly hinting at that in the event.


That being said, let's talk about Maya before the accident. This isn't the first time I've written about it. I think the answer is actually really simple:

We learned from Himiwari that wishes don't really affect YOU, but another you in the next universe over(essentially).

If Akira wished for Maya, she wouldn't just start existing in the next universe; Instead, that universe would change so that Maya always existed.

That's why she was there before the accident. In that universe, she always existed as a way to help protect Akira when Sekai eventually dies.
